_comment: Nepali given names and surnames, which no registry publishes.
Nepal has no equivalent of INSEE or the US Census surname file -- and neither does
India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka or Bangladesh. India's Census publishes around two hundred
tables under GODL and not one of them counts names. That absence is why South Asia
leans on Wikidata here while France, Spain, Poland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Slovenia,
Israel and Taiwan each have a national source.
This set is aggregate popularity -- how many people hold a name -- and not a roster of
people, which is the line that disqualified every other candidate found alongside it:
one built from a leaked Facebook dump, one from 'public records', one from unnamed
datasets, one scraped from Wiktionary and therefore CC BY-SA whatever its repository
says.
It is CC0, and it is compiled from Wikipedia's lists of most common names. A scraper
cannot relicense its upstream, so what makes CC0 defensible here is that the extracted
content is facts nobody authored -- that Chaudhary is a common surname in Nepal -- the
same reasoning behind the `public-facts` label used elsewhere in this directory. The
licence is recorded as the publisher states it and the provenance is recorded here, so
the judgement is visible rather than implied.
Only Nepal is taken. Sri Lanka has fifty surnames and no given names at all, so a
locale for it would answer entirely in English -- the same reason Telugu, Marathi and
Odia have no locale. India is covered better by Wikidata's Hindi, which carries 211
given names against this file's twenty.
Nepali is written in Devanagari and these names are romanised. That is a deliberate
trade: the file's Nepali surnames carry both scripts but its given names are Latin
only, and pairing Devanagari surnames with Latin given names is the chimera this
corpus refuses. All-Latin is coherent, and romanised Nepali names are what passports,
airline systems and English-language records actually hold.
